zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (supplied page subset). It is a contextual cross-check, not the authority for this scan's letters, accents, or typography. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Taihin is an important or honoured guest, matching ōkina marebito. The Portuguese hon- continues as honrado; the last consonant is n rather than the draft's m.
Rado completes honrado, and hoſpede supplies guest. The upright S. marks the entry as written usage.
Taihō is equated with ōkatadono and refers here to noble women. The final specification on the next row restricts the definition to widows.
The women are widows. The scan prints the double-u form viuuas; it is not shortened to the draft's viuas or modernized to viúvas.
Taifū is a great wind or storm, paraphrased by ōkaze. The physical line ends with a hyphen in tempeſta-, not the OCR's period.
De completes tempestade. The example says that the great wind moves the waves, then explains dōzuru by ugokasu, divided Vgo- / caſu.
Caſu completes ugokasu. The Portuguese translates the action as the great wind raising large waves; the historical aleuanta is retained.
Ondas completes the storm example's object. This short line is body text, separate from the following Taigai entry.
Taigai refers to things in general or for the most part, with oyoso no koto as its paraphrase. The vowel after ſ is o, not the OCR's i.
The alternative gloss is approximately, a little more or less. This completes the range of Taigai rather than adding a new example.
Taigan concerns meeting face to face; the Japanese paraphrase invokes facing countenances. The worn internal vowel of cauobaxe is read as a rather than e; the Portuguese encontrar-se continues below.
The Portuguese completes meeting someone. The scan joins Taiganſuru, and the example is not respaced to match a modern analysis.

runs.text: Certa doença de molheres que ſe va-

lines.note: Taige names a historical category of women's illness described here through loss of blood. The note explains the printed gloss without imposing a modern medical diagnosis.
The bleeding description completes vazão. The compound Taigue bôrô is given as equivalent; the weakened initial of bôrô is read with the compound, not changed to an apparent t.
Taigen denotes a strong beneficial effect, described as great improvement. The following row specifies recovery from illness.
The example expresses having obtained a substantial improvement. Yemǒxi- continues as yemōshita below; the printed caron is retained.

runs.text: Recebi grande melhoria, ou eſtou mui-

lines.note: Ta completes the Japanese past-tense example. The Portuguese says that the speaker received great improvement or is much better; mui- continues below.
To completes muito, and milhor is the printed historical form for better. This line finishes the recovery example.
Taigenno and taigenna describe a great fool. The paired forms and their doubled n are retained as printed, without imposing modern word formation.
This taigi is a great lie, equated with ōkina itsuwari. The final S. is an upright usage label, not part of the italic gloss.
This homograph denotes a great, burdensome, or difficult matter. The explanatory Vôqinarugui is printed together and remains so, although it can be analysed into separate Japanese elements.
The definition completes the three alternatives: a great thing, a laborious thing, or a difficult thing. The small but visible word boundary in couſa trabalhoſa is restored.
Taigyo here is a large carriage, matching ōkina kuruma. The final o is unaccented, unlike the work entry two rows below.
This identically printed headword denotes a large fish. Vuo is the historical fish word uo, not an anomalous initial consonant to remove.
Taigyō is a great deed, work, or undertaking, paraphrased by ōkina shiwaza. The circumflex in Vôqina is faint but visible and restored to the draft.
Exercicio completes the work or practice definition. The upright S. supplies the written-use label.
Taigo means moving back or retreating, explained by ato e shirizoku. The Portuguese historical pera is preserved, and S. remains separate from the gloss.
Taigun denotes a large army. Ikusa supplies the explanatory military term rather than the exercise sense of the preceding Portuguese entry.
Taigun wo ugokasu means setting a large army in motion. The visible pilcrow and final hyphen are restored; grã- is not followed by a sentence-ending period.
De completes grande in the army description. The next example begins raising or assembling an army, with voco- continued below.
Su completes okosu, with moyōsu as an alternative. The Portuguese begins making or preparing the army; the Latin alternative marker is retained.

runs.text: grande exercito, ou mouer grande guerra.

lines.note: The definition adds preparing a large army or setting a great war in motion. The row completes the military examples without introducing a new headword.
Taiji means destroying or laying waste, equated with tairaguru. The Portuguese aſolar retains its printed single long s rather than being normalized.
Teki wo taiji suru means destroying enemies. The Portuguese initial syllable reads Deſ-, not the OCR's Doſ-, and the joined taigiſuru is retained.
Taijin here is withdrawal of the army or camp, paraphrased by jin wo shirizoku. The final letter is n, not u, making this distinct from the malformed hint Taigiu.
The army withdraws or breaks camp. Cito completes exercito; arrayal remains the printed historical spelling.
The second taijin means positioning an army opposite another. Mukatte jindoru explains taking up that facing position.
The opposing-armies description is completed. The example begins taijin wo toru, with toru divided at the physical line break.
Ru completes toru, while suru is offered as an alternative. The intervening marker is l, not i; the Portuguese describes setting up camp opposite the other.
The words complete the reference to the opposing camp. They remain an independent physical row despite their brevity.
Tai-i denotes a great physician, explained by ōkina isha. The internal hyphen separates the Japanese vowel sequence and is not a line-end division.

This homograph is the chief or essential matter. The example asks about the main point of Buddhist teaching; Buppôno is part of the Japanese sentence, not an embedded Portuguese term. The small terminal stroke after tai-i is weak; the draft's hyphen is retained rather than asserting a period.
The question asks what that essential point is. The Portuguese begins its matching question, with the remaining object and question mark on the next row.

Buppô completes the Portuguese question about the essence of Buddhist teaching. The printed o has a circumflex rather than the draft's grave; the unusual question mark followed by a period is retained.
Tai-in is glossed first as abundant male semen. The internal hyphen is visible and replaces the garbled Taiain; the next sense is introduced by abbreviated Itẽ.

runs.text: Grande luxuria que naſce da copia de ſemente.

lines.note: The second historical gloss is strong lust attributed to an abundance of semen. This records the dictionary's explanation without endorsing it as medical knowledge.
Taijin is an eminent or noble person, explained by ōkina hito. The damaged letters still support the complete headword, and the Portuguese prints the ß ligature in Peßoa.
Taijō is withdrawing from a castle or fortress, explained by shiro wo shirizoku. The Portuguese fortress noun is physically divided for- / taleza.
Taleza completes fortaleza. This short continuation remains a body line and does not belong to the tortoiseshell entry below.

runs.text: Costas da tartaruga de que fazem os

lines.note: Taimai is described through the turtle's shell or back, used as a material. The following line identifies the makers and their products.
The gloss says that Chinese craftsmen make various things or work from that material. Chinas is the printed Portuguese designation, not Japanese text.
Taiman means neglect or failing in something, matched by okotaru. The nasal abbreviation is retained, and S. is separated typographically as a usage label.

runs.text: Tochas, ou fachas de pinho, ou de

lines.note: Taimatsu denotes torches, including pine splints. This fuller headword corresponds to the torch meaning of Tai on the preceding page.
The torch can also be made from another material. The short line completes the material alternatives.
Taimei is explained literally as a great name and defined as a great noble lord. The printed initial T is not modernized to D.

runs.text: bre que rege a terra, ou q̃ tem algum officio co-

lines.note: Bre completes nobre. The noble either governs the land or holds an office, with the illustrative como divided at the end of this row.
Mo completes como. Vreadores is the historical printed form for councillors or civic officers; no extra vowel is supplied from modern Portuguese.
Taimen means meeting face to face, with omote ni mukau as its paraphrase. The Portuguese reads verſe, not OCR venſe.

runs.text: ſi, ou ver, ou encontrarſe depropoſito com al-

lines.note: The definition includes intentionally seeing or meeting someone. Joined depropoſito is preserved; the last word continues as alguem below.
Fitoni taimen suru gives the example of meeting a person. The Japanese construction completes the entry without a separate Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: Lugar onde ſe algũs vem, ou

lines.note: Taimenjo is a place for meeting or receiving visits. The final ou is clearly present at the right edge and restored to the draft.
Visitão completes the alternative action of visiting one another. The nasal mark is retained on its printed vowel.
Taimin is illustrated by Taiminkoku and equated with Taitō, referring to China. The faint t before the caroned o is restored from the scan; it is not the malformed Taiǒ of the draft.
No completes Reino, the kingdom of China. This is the Portuguese conclusion to the Taimin example, not a Japanese particle.
Taimō is great desire or aspiration, matching ōkina nozomi. The caroned o is preserved and corresponds to the related aspiration entry on the preceding page.
Tainai is inside the belly or womb, paraphrased by hara no uchi. The scan prints vchi, not the malformed vehi of the draft and its kana hint.
The example describes dwelling in the mother's womb. Fauano is retained as printed; the narrow letters in tainaini are separated correctly rather than collapsed into the OCR's tainami.
The Portuguese specifies being in the mother's womb. Mãy preserves the historical spelling and its nasal mark.
Tainō denotes a sack or bag. The upright S. is a register label, and the caron over o is not changed to a circumflex.

runs.text: Caſa interior onde estão as molheres

lines.note: Tai no ya is described as an inner residence where women stay. The Portuguese location continues on the next row.

The location is within the Dairi residence. On reinspection the whole embedded Japanese word is in italic, like the Portuguese around it; the draft's split roman D and italic airi is removed. Dairi is flagged as one exact whole-word term.
Taikei means great joy, explained by ōkina yorokobi. The entire Japanese paraphrase remains roman.
Taikei ni zonzuru expresses experiencing great joy. The narrow in sequence in Taiqeini corrects the OCR's m without changing the printed word boundary.

runs.text: Contenderem dous diante do juiz ſobre

lines.note: Taiketsu is a contest or dispute before a judge. The bare final t in the romanized headword is retained rather than expanded to tçu.

runs.text: algũa demanda, arrezoando cada hum por ſi.

lines.note: Each party argues its own case in the dispute. Arrezoando is one printed word, with doubled r; the final period is present at the right edge.
Taiki denotes a great or generous heart, matched by ōkina kokoro. The Portuguese character description continues below.

The sense is generous or liberal, followed by a person of great heart. The damaged consonant in expected liberal has a u-like surviving outline, so liueral is retained with this caveat rather than silently supplying a full b.
Ção completes coração. Magnifico adds nobility or magnificence of character to the description.
This homograph is a large vessel, matching ōkina utsuwamono. The Portuguese alternative vaſilha is physically divided after va-.
Silha completes vaſilha, giving a large container. This short line is part of the vessel entry, not the guest-hosting entry that follows.

runs.text: O ter algum hoſpede em caſa.

lines.note: Taikyaku is receiving or having a guest at home. The final S. is the upright written-register label.
Taikyo is the great sky or open air, with ōzora as the Japanese equivalent and Ar as the brief Portuguese gloss.
Taikyoku is described as a first principle comparable to prime matter. The note records the dictionary's philosophical comparison rather than treating it as a modern scientific claim.

runs.text: teria prima de que tratão certos Philoſophos da

lines.note: Teria completes materia. The explanation attributes discussion of this first principle to certain philosophers of China, continued below.
China completes the philosophical entry. At far right, bição and its S. label belong semantically to the next entry's prohibição; they remain on their actual physical row as displaced text.
Taikin is a great prohibition or injunction, matching ōkina imashime. Prohi takes the displaced bição above; the weak ascender is read as h, not OCR b, and no line-end hyphen is invented.
The adjectival form taikina refers back to Taiqi above. The referenced Japanese word is embedded in the cross-reference apparatus and is flagged for whole-word font review.
Taikwa denotes excess, explained by greatly exceeding. The initial of ſuguru is long s, not f; the Portuguese gloss also contrasts excess with shortage below.
The paired expression contrasts excess and insufficiency. The scan supports fuguiǔ, with gui rather than the OCR's gur; its final u mark remains a caron.
Ceßo completes excesso, opposed to lack or scarcity. The printed ß and the absence of a comma after falta are retained.
This taikwa is a serious fault or offence, paraphrased by ōkina toga. The next line completes the alternative Portuguese noun and starts an example.
The example says that permitting a small fault leads to a great one. The conditional reads yuruxeba, not the OCR's yuruxoba; xǒqua and taiqua form the small/great contrast.

runs.text: O deixar de castigar hum pequeno

lines.note: To naru completes becoming a great fault. The Portuguese interprets allowing the small fault as neglecting to punish it.

runs.text: peccado he ocaſão de ſe fazerem grandes pec-

lines.note: The translation says that an unpunished small sin gives occasion for great sins. Its last word continues into the restored cados. body row, not the catchword.
Cados completes peccados from the preceding row. This is genuine body text mistakenly combined with the catchword in the provisional furniture; it is restored with a new stable ID.

The catchword anticipates Taiquai on the next page. Its middle letters are abraded, especially the first i; the adopted reading follows surviving strokes and the independently printed entry, not the OCR fragments.
